name: hermetica_01
title: Poimandres, the Shepherd of Men
description: The visionary opening revelation of the Corpus Hermeticum: Hermes beholds the Mind of the Universe, the Man-Shepherd, who reveals the creation of the cosmos and the nature of God as Light and Life.
text: 1. It chanced once on a time my mind was meditating on the things that are, my thought was raised to a great height, the senses of my body being held back—just as men are who are weighed down with sleep after a fill of food, or from fatigue of body. Methought a Being more than vast, in size beyond all bounds, called out my name and saith: What wouldst thou hear and see, and what hast thou in mind to learn and know? I am Man-Shepherd, Mind of all-masterhood; I know what thou desirest and I'm with thee everywhere. I reply: I long to learn the things that are, and comprehend their nature, and know God. Then saith to me Man-Shepherd: That Light am I, thy God, Mind, prior to Moist Nature which appeared from Darkness; the Light-Word that appeared from Mind is Son of God. Not separate are they the one from other; just in their union rather is it Life consists.
notes: The foundational Hermetic revelation. Poimandres = the Mind of Sovereignty.

name: hermetica_02
title: The General Sermon
description: The General Sermon on God and creation. (The text is lost in the original Greek but summarized through the Corpus's remaining teachings.)
text: NOTE: The title only is preserved in our Corpus, the text having disappeared with the loss of a quire or quires before the parent copy came into the hands of Psellus. However, Hermes teaches throughout the Corpus that: The Glory of all things is God, Godhead and Godly Nature. Source of the things that are is God, who is both Mind and Nature—yea Matter, the Wisdom that reveals all things. Source too is Godhead—yea Nature, Energy, Necessity, and End, and Making-new-again. For God is the All, and the All is God. What is above the heavens is God; what is below the heavens is the All. The Good is in God alone; and the Cosmos is the Plenitude of God, while God is the Good of the Cosmos.
notes: Text lost from the original Corpus — only the title preserved by Psellus.

name: hermetica_03
title: The Sacred Sermon of Hermes to Asclepius
description: A sacred discourse on creation: the Glory of God as the Source of all things, the emergence of Light from the Abyss, and the ordering of the cosmos through the seven circles of Heaven.
text: III. (IV.) The Sacred Sermon of Hermes to Asclepius: The Glory of all things is God, Godhead and Godly Nature. Source of the things that are is God, who is both Mind and Nature—yea Matter, the Wisdom that reveals all things. Darkness that knew no bounds was in Abyss, and Water too and subtle Breath intelligent; these were by Power of God in Chaos. Then Holy Light arose; and there collected 'neath Dry Space from out Moist Essence Elements. And Heaven was seen in seven circles; its Gods were visible in forms of stars with all their signs; while Nature had her members made articulate together with the Gods in her. And every God by his own proper power brought forth what was appointed him. Thus there arose four-footed beasts, and creeping things, and those that in the water dwell, and things with wings.
notes: Corpus Hermeticum III (IV.) — sometimes called the Sacred Sermon.

name: hermetica_04
title: The Cup or Monad
description: Hermes teaches Tat about the divine Mind: God's body is invisible and immeasurable, and He sent forth a Cup filled with Mind as a prize for souls who have faith to ascend.
text: IV. (V.) The Cup or Monad of Hermes to Tat: With Reason, not with hands, did the World-maker make the universal World; so that thou thus shouldst think of Him as everywhere and ever-being, the Author of all things, and One and Only, who by His Will all beings hath created. This Body of Him is a thing no man can touch, or see, or measure, a Body inextensible, like to no other frame. 'Tis neither Fire nor Water, Air nor Breath; yet all of them come from it. Now being Good He willed to consecrate this Body to Himself alone. He tilled a mighty Cup with Mind, and sent it down, joining a Herald to it, to whom He gave command to make this proclamation: Baptize thyself with this Cup's draught, thou who art able, thou who hast faith that thou shalt return to Him who sent the Cup.
notes: Corpus Hermeticum IV (V.) — the baptism of Mind.

name: hermetica_05
title: The Key
description: Hermes' discourse to Tat on God as Father and the Good: God's energy is His Will, and His essence is to will the being of all things. The Good alone is the creator; the Cosmos shares in the Good only through participation.
text: X. (XI.) The Key of Thrice-Greatest Hermes: God, Father and the Good, hath the same nature, or more exactly, energy. God's energy is then His Will; further His essence is to will the being of all things. For what is God and Father and the Good but the to be of all that are not yet? Nay, subsistence self of everything that is—this, then, is God, this Father, this the Good; to Him is added naught of all the rest. And though the Cosmos, that is to say the Sun, is also sire himself to them that share in him; yet so far is he not the cause of good unto the lives, he is not even of their living. So that even if he be a sire, he is entirely so by the compulsion of the Good's Good-will, apart from which nor being nor becoming could ever be.
notes: Corpus Hermeticum X (XI.) — the abridgment of the General Sermons.

name: hermetica_06
title: In God Alone is Good
description: A sermon to Asclepius on the transcendence of the Good: Good is in none else save God alone. The Good is essence free from motion and becoming; all things subject to birth abound in passions and cannot partake of the Good.
text: VI. (VII.) In God Alone is Good and Elsewhere Nowhere: Good, O Asclepius, is in none else save God alone; nay, rather, Good is God Himself eternally. If it be so, Good must be essence, from every kind of motion and becoming free, possessed of stable energy around Itself, never too little, nor too much, an ever-full supply. Though one, yet is It source of all; for what supplieth all is Good. But this belongs to no one else save God alone. For He stands not in need of any thing, so that desiring it He should be bad; nor can a single thing of things that are be lost to Him, on losing which He should be pained. For things subject to birth abound in passions, birth in itself being passible. But where there's passion, nowhere is there Good.
notes: Corpus Hermeticum VI (VII.) — the Good as the sole attribute of God.

name: hermetica_07
title: The Secret Sermon on the Mountain
description: Tat beseeches Hermes for the teaching on Rebirth. Hermes reveals that the seed of regeneration is the True Good, the womb is Wisdom-in-Silence, and the sower is the Will of God.
text: XIII. (XIV.) The Secret Sermon on the Mountain Concerning Rebirth and the Promise of Silence: Tat saith: In the General Sermons, father, thou didst speak in riddles most unclear, conversing on Divinity; and when thou saidst no man could ever be saved before Rebirth, thy meaning thou didst hide. I know not from out what matter and what womb Man comes to birth, or of what seed. Hermes saith: Wisdom that understands in silence—such is the matter and the womb from out which Man is born, and the True Good the seed. Tat saith: Who is the sower? Hermes saith: It is the Will of God, my son. The one that is begot will be another one from God, God's Son. Hermes saith: All in all, out of all powers composed. Now, my son, keep silence and the birth divine shall be perfected in thee.
notes: Corpus Hermeticum XIII (XIV.) — the mystery of palingenesis.

name: hermetica_08
title: The Perfect Sermon (Asclepius I)
description: The first part of the Asclepius, or Perfect Sermon: Hermes teaches Asclepius about God, the One and the All, and the eye of intellect that alone can see the Divine Word.
text: II. The Perfect Sermon or the Asclepius, Part I: God, O Asclepius, hath brought thee unto us that thou mayest hear a Godly sermon, a sermon such as well may seem of all the previous ones we've either uttered, or with which we've been inspired by the Divine, more Godly than the piety of ordinary faith. If thou with eye of intellect shalt see this Word thou shalt in thy whole mind be filled quite full of all things good. If that, indeed, the many be the good, and not the one, in which are all. Indeed the difference between the two is found in their agreement—All is of One or One is All. So closely bound is each to other, that neither can be parted from its mate.
notes: The Asclepius (Latin original lost; survives in Latin translation only). Part I.

name: hermetica_09
title: The Perfect Sermon (Asclepius II)
description: The concluding teachings of the Perfect Sermon: the Aeon as God's image, the Cosmos as the Aeon's image, and the prophecy of the passing of the old order when God will restore all things.
text: The Perfect Sermon or the Asclepius, conclusion: O Asclepius, the Aeon is God's image, while Cosmos is the Aeon's image; the Sun is Cosmos' image, while Man is Sun's image. All things depend on the will of God. The Master of Eternity is God, who is one, and who is all. He has filled all things with His presence. He is the Father of all things, and the Good of all things, and the Life of all things. For this is the glory of all things—that God should be present in them. But the time draws near when men shall think that God is powerless; shall count the Cosmos unworthy of their reverence. Then shall the old order pass away, and God shall restore all things to their pristine beauty.
notes: Asclepius conclusion — includes the famous Hermetic prophecy of the fall of Egypt.

name: hermetica_10
title: The Definitions of Asclepius
description: Asclepius writes to King Ammon defining the All: a summing up of all Hermetic teachings. A warning against translation into Greek, and an invocation to God who, though being All, is One.
text: (XVI.) The Definitions of Asclepius unto King Ammon: Great is the sermon which I send to thee, O King—the summing up and digest, as it were, of all the rest. For it is not composed to suit the many's prejudice, since it contains much that refuteth them. Hermes, my master, hath said that unto those who come across my books, their composition will seem most simple and clear; but as 'tis unclear, and has the inner meaning of its words concealed, it will be still unclearer when the Greeks will want to turn our tongue into their own. The Greeks have novel words, energic of argumentation only; but we do not use words, but use sounds full-filled with deeds. Thus will I begin by invocation unto God, the universals' Lord and Maker, who though being All is One.
notes: Corpus Hermeticum (XVI.) — Asclepius' letter to King Ammon.
